workEn: The Secret History of the Mongols
title: 元朝秘史 §§249–252
titleEn: The Secret History of the Mongols — §§249–252: Tangut Camels, the Pass at Tongguan and the Spoils of Zhongdu
part: §§249–252 — Tangut Camels, the Pass at Tongguan and the Spoils of Zhongdu
source: Mongγol-un niγuča tobčiyan (The Secret History of the Mongols), §§249–252, in the Ming Chinese-character phonetic transcription, as edited with a romanized reading by Shiratori Kurakichi 白鳥庫吉, 音訳蒙文元朝秘史 (Tokyo, 1943), itself based on the Ye Dehui 葉德輝 printed edition of 1905/1908; text taken from the Japanese Wikisource transcription, archived and verified against it character for character. Shiratori died in 1942, so the edition was public domain in Japan before the URAA date and was never restored in the United States. Section numbering (§) is the standard citation system. Romanization convention: Shiratori's, kept exactly as he prints it (γ, ġ, ṅ, ž, č, and the raised dot of γ̇). Translations are made fresh from the Mongolian, with the Ming interlinear Chinese glosses as the primary crib. No modern translation was consulted. langCode is null: there is no text-to-speech for Middle Mongol.
about: Burqan of the Qashin submits to Chinggis, gives him his daughter Chaqa and promises camels, cloth and hawks (§249); the sheep-year campaign brings the Altan Qan of the Kitad and the Tangut leader Iluqu-Burqan to submission (§250); in the dog year, after the Altan Qan blocks the envoys to the Song, Chinggis goes against the Jin by the Tongguan pass while Jebe takes Chabchiyal, Ile, Qada and Höbögetür are beaten, and the Altan Qan flees Zhongdu for Nanjing (§251); at Zhongdu three men count the treasure, and Shigi-Qutuqu alone refuses Qada’s gifts and is praised for it (§252). Grammar to watch: long converb chains in -žu/-žü; possessives in -tei/-tü/-tai/-ten; the reflexive -(i)jen; passives in -gde-; the ese/ülü pair of negatives; and the Ming glossators’ Chinese place names and titles (Zhongdu, Hexiwu, liushou).
draftNote: The Mongol readings follow Shiratori throughout; the English is a first drafting.

sentences.l: That, mounting-as, Qashin people-to set-out.
sentences.i: He mounted and set out for the Qashin people.
sentences.n: jorčiba (jorči- ‘set out’, from the Ming 去 alone, + past -ba) is the verb; everything before it is setting. morilaγsaγ̇ar is mori ‘horse’ + -la- + an ending -γsaγ̇ar that the Ming glosses 依着 ‘according to’; I read ‘as soon as he had mounted’ loosely and am not sure of the ending. irge-dür is irgen ‘people’ with its n lost before the hyphen + dative-locative -dür (Ming 行, ‘to’). The subject is not named: ‘he’ is taken to be Chinggis, who first appears in the fourth unit of this section, and the Ming 那 ‘that’ (tere) is left out of the English.

sentences.t: Žorižü kürüġesü Qašin irgen-ü Burqan elsen

morph.gloss: to aim at, point at, set out for [指着]
Qashin, a people or land (Ming 種名 ‘kind, tribe’) [種(名)]

sentences.l: Aiming, when-arriving, Qashin people’s Burqan submitting,
sentences.i: Making for them, and when he arrived, Burqan of the Qashin people submitted,
sentences.n: Two converbs open a chain: žorižü (žori- ‘aim at’, + -žü; Ming 指着) and kürüġesü (kürü- ‘arrive’ + conditional -ġesü, Ming 呵, ‘when/if he arrived’). Qašin irgen-ü Burqan is ‘the Qashin people’s Burqan’: the possessor stands before its noun. Ming 人名 makes Burqan a man here, not the mountain. elsen is else- ‘submit’ + converb -n (Ming 歸附); it can also be the noun ‘submission’, so ‘Burqan [came in] submission’ is possible. Shiratori puts no marks round the offer that follows; I supply them in `i` only.

morph.gloss: you (second-person singular; stem čin- before case endings) [你的]
genitive: of (after the n of a stem; back-vowel form)
optative: let it be …, I will …

sentences.l: right hand your becoming, strength I-will-give, saying
sentences.i: saying, “I will be your right hand and give you my strength.”
sentences.n: Converb chain again: bolžu ‘becoming’ hands its sense on to ögsü, the optative (ög- ‘give’ + -sü; Ming 與我 ‘I will give’), and keġen (keġe- ‘say’ + -n) closes the quotation, as the Ming 麽道 does. čin-u is či ‘you’ in its oblique stem + genitive, ‘your’. ‘Right hand’ is in the Ming (右 手); that it means a chief support is my reading of the idiom, not something the Ming says.

sentences.t: Čaqa neretei öki Čiṅgis Qaγ̇an-a γarγažu ögbe.

morph.gloss: Chinggis, the title borne by Temüjin from 1206 [太祖︀]

sentences.l: Chaqa named daughter, Chinggis Qaγan-to bringing-out, gave.
sentences.i: He brought out a daughter named Chaqa and gave her to Chinggis Qahan.
sentences.n: Possessive -tei (nere ‘name’ + -tei, Ming 名有的, ‘name-having’): ‘a daughter, Chaqa by name’; the -tei/-tü pair follows vowel harmony (neretü appears at §250). Qaγ̇an-a is the dative-locative -a (Ming 行), ‘to the Qahan’. γarγažu is γar- ‘go out’ + causative -γa- + -žu (Ming 出着), ‘making go out’: a daughter led out of the household. The subject is not named; Burqan is the only candidate, and the next unit names him again.

sentences.i: Burqan Qan spoke again:
sentences.n: ügülerün (ügüle- ‘speak’ + -rün ‘while …ing’, Ming 說) serves as the frame verb, as in earlier parts. Qān (Ming 皇帝) is the short title form beside qaγan, so this is Burqan with a title, ‘Burqan Qan’. The speech opens at the next unit, on Shiratori’s mark at Čiṅgis, and runs to the mark after asuγai.

sentences.i: “Hearing the name and fame of Chinggis Qahan, we had been afraid.
sentences.n: Two converbs, sonosču ‘hearing’ and ajužu ‘fearing’, run into alaγ̇ai. alaγ̇ai: the Ming 有來 ‘was, had been’ makes this a- ‘be’ + a past ending -laγ̇ai (compare abulaγ̇a, Ming 了來), not ala- ‘kill’ as an older glossary entry has it for another line; I am not sure of the ending. ba (Ming 俺) is ‘we’ and stands after the verb, closing the clause. nere aldar, ‘name, fame’, are set side by side with no ‘and’.

genitive: of (after the n of a stem; back-vowel form)

sentences.l: Now majesty-having body your arriving, having-been-come-to, from-majesty feared.
sentences.i: Now your majestic person has arrived, and we, having been come upon, were afraid of its majesty.
sentences.n: šüldertü is sülder ‘majesty’ (Ming 威靈, ‘awesome spirit’; elsewhere ‘omen’) + possessive -tü, ‘majesty-having’: the same possessive pattern as neretei. kürčü is kür- ‘arrive’ + converb. iregdežü is ire- ‘come’ + passive -gde- + -žü (Ming 被來着): the passive turns ‘he came to us’ into ‘we were come to’, which I give as ‘come upon’. sülder-eče is the ablative -eče, ‘from/of’; the ablative after a verb of fear means ‘afraid of’. The Ming glosses the last word 怕了, ‘feared’ (ajuba, past).

sentences.l: Fearing, we Tangut people right hand your becoming, strength I-will-give said.
sentences.i: Being afraid, we, the Tangut people, said, ‘We will be your right hand and give you strength.’
sentences.n: keġebe (keġe- ‘say’ + -be, Ming 說了) sits inside the speech: Burqan recalls what ‘we’ said, which is the same offer as in the third unit. ba (Ming 俺) is ‘we’ here at the head of the clause. Shiratori has no inner marks; the single quotes are mine. Qašin and Taṅγ̇ud (both Ming 種(名)) are both used for Burqan’s people; I do not equate them beyond what the text does. Taṅγ̇ud has the plural -d.

sentences.t: Küčü ögürün nunži nutuγtan nödügsen balaγasutan bi-že.

sentences.l: Strength when-giving, unmoving camp-having built town-having are-indeed.
sentences.i: When we give you strength, we are settled people, with camps that do not move and towns that are built.
sentences.n: Possessive plural: nutuγtan and balaγasutan are nutuγ ‘camp’ (Ming 營盤) and balaγasun ‘town’ + -tan, ‘those having’ (the back-vowel companion of -ten; the n of balaγasun is lost). nunži (Ming 不動的 ‘unmoving’, stem unclear) and nödügsen (Ming 築的 ‘built’, stem inferred) describe them. The point, taken up in the next unit, is that settled folk cannot move fast. ögürün is ög- ‘give’ + -ürün (Ming 與時 ‘when giving’). bi-že is bü- ‘be’ as bi- before -že (Ming 有也者), ‘are indeed’.

sentences.l: Companions-being, swift campaigning, at-the-time-of-campaigning, sharp fighting, at-the-time-of-fighting, swift campaign-in, chasing indeed unable-indeed.
sentences.i: As your companions, at times of swift marching out and of sharp fighting, we are indeed unable to give chase on a swift campaign.
sentences.n: Hard. The frame is nököčežü ‘being companions’ (from nökör) and a closing jadamui-že (jada- ‘be unable’, stem from the Ming 不能, + present -müi + particle -že, ‘indeed’). aja (Ming 征進 ‘march out’) is a bare form I cannot analyse; ajalaqui-dur is aja + -la- + participle -qui + -dur (Ming 時 ‘at the time of’), and bulγalduqui-dur is bulγa- ‘fight’ + reciprocal -ldu- + -qui + -dur in the same way. qurdun ‘swift’, qurča ‘sharp’ (Ming 鋒利). güjičen-že is güjiče- ‘chase, overtake’ (the glossary’s stem, from the Ming 趕上; here Ming 趕) + converb -n + -že. ‘We cannot keep up’ is the sense I reach; whether it is a confession or an excuse for offering camels instead of soldiers is for the next units to show.

sentences.l: Chinggis Qaγan-acc when-favouring, we Tangut people, high deresün-grass’s shelter-in bringing-up, many camels bringing-out, qa making, I-will-give.
sentences.i: If Chinggis Qahan shows us favour, we, the Tangut people, will rear many camels in the shelter of the tall deresün grass, bring them out, make them state property (qa), and give them.
sentences.n: A converb chain behind a conditional: sojurγaγ̇asu (sojurγa- ‘show favour’ + -γ̇asu, Ming 恩賜呵) opens it, ösgežü ‘bringing up’, γarγažu ‘bringing out’ and bolγažu ‘making’ follow, and ögsü ‘I will give’ ends it. Qaγ̇an-i has the accusative, which the Ming 行 glosses as it does -a and -dur; I read it as the one favouring, ‘if Chinggis Qahan favours’, and supply ‘us’. ündür ‘high’ stands before its noun. deresün (Ming 蓆棘草) is a tall steppe grass and nemüre-de is nemüre ‘cover, shelter’ (Ming 遮護, stem inferred) + -de: harmony, -ü after deresün, -de not -da. temeġed is temeġe ‘camel’ + -d. qa (Ming 係官) means ‘belonging to the officials’, that is, to the state; I give ‘make them state property’ from the Ming and keep the word qa beside it, but the Mongol sense is not certain.

sentences.t: Örmege nekežü aγ̇urasun bolγažu ögsü.

morph.gloss: to weave (stem read from the Ming 織; a different Ming, 追趕, elsewhere) [織着]
bolt of cloth (Ming 段匹) [段匹]
optative: let it be …, I will …

sentences.l: Woollen-stuff weaving, cloth-bolts making, I-will-give.
sentences.i: We will weave woollen cloth, have it made into bolts, and give it.
sentences.n: örmege (Ming 氁子) is a woollen stuff, aγ̇urasun (Ming 段匹) a bolt of cloth. nekežü: the Ming 織着 ‘weaving’ fixes the sense here; the same spelling elsewhere has 追趕 ‘pursue’, so the stem is borrowed from the sound and the Ming. bolγažu is the causative again, ‘having them made’. The closing ögsü, ‘I will give’, is a refrain that ends each offer.

to train, teach (Ming 調 ‘tame, break in’) [調着]

sentences.l: Releasable hawks training, gathering, the-good-ones his having-sent, always" saying, reported.
sentences.i: “We will train hawks for flying, gather the good ones, and have them sent to him without fail,” he reported.
sentences.n: The closing mark of the speech is on asuγai. oγ̇orqu is a participle in -qu (Ming 放的 ‘to be let go’), so ‘hawks to be released’; šibaγ̇un has the Ming 鷹, a hawk. said-i is sai ‘good’ + plural -d + accusative -i, ‘the good ones’. in-ü is the third-person genitive set after its noun, ‘his’ (Ming 他的): I read it as Chinggis, hence ‘to him’, but the Ming does not say. asuγai is a- ‘be’ + -suγai (optative) elsewhere; here the Ming 常川 ‘constantly’ decides. keġen öčibe: ‘saying, reported’ (öči-, Ming 奏, report to a superior).

sentences.t: Ügüležü üge-dür(i)-jen kürün
sentences.l: Speaking, to-word-his-own arriving,
sentences.i: Having spoken, and coming up to his own words,
sentences.n: kürün is kür- ‘arrive’ + converb -n; üge-dür(i)-jen is üge ‘word’ + dative-locative -dür + reflexive -(i)jen, ‘his own’ (the (i) is Shiratori’s). Literally ‘arriving at his own word’; the Ming gives only 到 ‘arrive’, so I keep to the grammar, ‘coming up to his own words’; that he made good what he had said is the likely sense, but the Ming does not say it.

to levy, gather in (Ming 科斂 ‘levy’) [科斂着]

sentences.l: Tangut people from-own camels levying, driving until-unable, bringing-along, gave.
sentences.i: he levied camels from his own Tangut people and, driving them until they could drive no more, brought them in and gave them.
sentences.n: Reflexive on a case ending: irgen-eče-ġen is irgen ‘people’ + ablative -eče + -ġen, ‘from his own people’. qubčižu is qubči- ‘levy’ (Ming 科斂 ‘collect’) + -žu. taγ̇un jadatala (Ming 趕 不能直(到)) I read as ‘driving until unable [to drive more]’, that is, as many as could be driven; taγ̇un is the glossary’s daγ̇u- ‘drive along’ (printed with t), a stem inferred from the Ming and jadatala is jada- ‘be unable’ + -tala ‘until’. abčiražü (ab- ‘take’ plus a second verb, form uncertain) I give loosely as ‘brought in’. The subject, Burqan, is not repeated.

sentences.l: Chinggis Qaγan that mounting-at, Kitad people’s Altan Qaγan-acc making-submit, many cloth-bolts taking,
sentences.i: When Chinggis Qahan took the field on that occasion, he made the Altan Qahan of the Kitad people submit, and took many bolts of cloth,
sentences.n: morilaγsan-dur is mori + -la- + past participle -γsan + -dur (Ming 上馬時): ‘at the time of having mounted’, which I give as ‘took the field’. elšeġülžü is else- ‘submit’ (printed elše-) + causative -ġül- + -žü (Ming 敎歸附着, ‘causing to submit’). Kitad is the Ming 契丹, but here it names the Jin state and its people; Altan (Ming 金) is ‘gold’ and the Jin ruler’s title. No finite verb ends this chain: the sentence starts over at Čiṅgis, two units on, with the same events told again in more detail.

sentences.l: Qashin people’s Burqan-acc making-submit, many camels taking,
sentences.i: made Burqan of the Qashin people submit, and took many camels;
sentences.n: Parallel to the unit before: the object is Burqan-(n)i, with Shiratori’s bracketed (n) of the accusative, and the spoil is camels where the Jin’s was cloth. This is the Burqan of §249 (the same word, Ming 人名行), but the text then gives the Tangut a second leader, Iluqu-Burqan, a few units on; I leave unsettled whether the two are one man.

sentences.n: Hard. baražu is bara- ‘be finished, used up’ (Ming 了着) + -žu, so Elsen baražu is something like ‘the submission being done’, and I give it that way; it could instead mean that the speaker had finished taking the submission of another. sentences.i: As for Chinggis Qahan, he came by the Tongguan pass.
sentences.n: Qaγ̇an-i has the accusative with a verb that takes no object (the Ming 行 only glosses the ending), so I read it as a topic, ‘as for the Qahan’. bolba ‘became’ is the empty verb of the unit before, here with the instrumental, ‘made his way by’. sentences.n: Ile and Qada are men’s names here (Ming 人名), not ile ‘openly’ or qada ‘cliff’. γurban-a is γurban ‘three’ + dative-locative -a (Ming 三箇人行). medeġülžü is mede- ‘know’ + causative -ġül- + -žü (Ming 敎管着), ‘making [them] manage’: ‘put in charge’, as in the house rendering of medeġülbe. sentences.n: The Altan Qan’s order opens at Shiratori’s mark on čerig. Hard: bögležü (bögle-, Ming 塞着 ‘stop up, fill’, stem inferred) has no stated object, and I supply ‘it’, the pass of the next unit. maṅlailan is maṅlai ‘front, van’ + -la- + converb -n (Ming 爲頭, ‘at the head’); Hulaγ̇an-Degelen-i has the accusative and the Ming 種(名)行, so it is a people’s name, which I write Hula’an-Degelen (γ̇ becomes ’ in names). Whether it is part of the Jin’s army or the Kitad’s I cannot say. žasažu is žasa- ‘put in order’ (Ming 整治着).

sentences.i: contest the Tongguan pass, and do not let them cross the ridge!” he said,
sentences.n: Closing mark of the order is on dabaγ̇uludqun. bu ‘do not’ (Ming 休) is the prohibitive. dabaγ̇a (Ming 嶺) ‘ridge, pass’ and the verb daba- ‘cross’ make a figure: ‘do not cross the crossing’. Because the Ming has the causative, ‘do not let them cross’ is my reading; ‘do not cross’ addressed to the troops is also possible.

sentences.n: iležüġüi is ile- ‘send’ + -žüġüi (a final past; Ming 敎去了, ‘caused to go’). Kitad-un has the genitive -un (back-vowel form). γažar ‘land’ is followed by keġen ‘saying’ (Ming 地 麽道), so the Mongol has a quoted word; whose land is meant, and who speaks, the Ming does not tell, and the quotation marks are mine. daγ̇ažu (Ming 當着 ‘confront’) I read as daγa- ‘bear, withstand’ (the glossary has daγa- ‘bear’ and daγus- ‘withstand’, Ming 當的); the link is uncertain. irebe ‘came’.

sentences.l: Chinggis Qaγan Hexiwu-acc having-come-down, Zhongdu’s Shira-Keger came-down.
sentences.i: Chinggis Qahan encamped at Hexiwu, and then at Zhongdu’s Shira-Keger.
sentences.n: baγ̇uγ̇ad and baγ̇uba are the verb baγ̇u- ‘come down’ twice, as converb and then finite; ‘encamp’ is my reading of what a Qahan does in coming down at a place, as at Sa’ari-Keger in §250. Hosiwü-ji (Ming 鎭名, Han 河西務) is a garrison-town, with the accusative -ji; the Han reads Hexiwu. Žuṅdu-jin is the genitive -jin after a vowel, ‘Zhongdu’s’; Šira-Keġer is a place-name (Ming 地名).

sentences.t: Žebe Čabčijal-un qālγa ebdežü

morph.gloss: pass, gate (printed qālγa; Ming 關) [關]

sentences.l: Jebe Chabchiyal’s pass breaking,
sentences.i: Jebe broke the Chabchiyal pass,
sentences.n: Čabčijal-un is the genitive -un (back-vowel form), ‘of Chabchiyal’; qālγa (Ming 關, with a long ā) is the gate or pass; ebdežü is ebde- ‘break’ + -žü (Ming 破着). The converb chain runs on into the next unit.

sentences.t: Čabčijal-i bariγsad čeriġüd-i ködölgežü irežü Čiṅgis Qaγan-dur neilebe.

sentences.l: Chabchiyal-acc holding troops-acc driving, coming, Chinggis Qaγan-to joined.
sentences.i: marched on the troops who held Chabchiyal, came up, and joined Chinggis Qahan.
sentences.n: bariγsad is bari- ‘seize, hold’ + the plural participle -γsad (Ming 把的每), ‘those who held’, with Čabčijal-i as its object; čeriġüd-i is the troops with plural and accusative. Whose troops these are is not said: they may be the garrison Jebe has just put in the pass, since they then ‘come up’ to join the Qahan; I give ‘marched’ and not ‘drove’ so as not to make them an enemy. ködölgežü ‘setting in motion’ (Ming 推動着) as at §251, here ‘drove on’. Qaγan-dur is the dative-locative (Ming 行), and neilebe (neile- ‘join’, Ming 相合) takes it: ‘joined with’.

sentences.i: When the Altan Qan went out from Zhongdu,
sentences.n: Žuṅdu-āča is the ablative -āča, ‘from Zhongdu’; γarurun is γar- ‘go out’ + -urun (Ming 出時 ‘when going out’). Shiratori prints an opening mark on Altan that nothing closes; the Ming gives no cue for speech and I read the sentence as narrative, as at §251.

sentences.i: he had made Qada the liushou inside Zhongdu, entrusting it to him, and had gone away.
sentences.n: Qada-ji (Ming 人名行) is the accusative -ji. The name is the same as the Qada of §251 and I do not say whether the two men are one. Liušu is Chinese, Han 留守, which the Ming leaves as (官名) ‘an official title’; I keep the Han’s reading ‘liushou’. bolγan is bol- + causative -γa- + -n, ‘making him’. tüšižü: Ming 委付着, ‘entrusting’. oduγsan ažuγ̇u is a participle plus ažuγ̇u (a- ‘be’ in the past), ‘had gone’, a pluperfect: a pattern that recurs.

sentences.i: Chinggis Qahan, while having the gold and silver, goods, bolts of cloth and so forth of Zhongdu counted,
sentences.n: toγ̇olaγ̇ulurun is toγ̇ola- ‘count’ + causative -γ̇ul- + -urun (Ming 敎數 ‘cause to count’): ‘while having [it] counted’, the -urun of time, not a purpose; the three men are sent in the next unit. altan ‘gold’ and müṅgün ‘silver’ (Ming 銀); ed is ‘goods, property’ (Ming 物); jaγ̇u-ke is jaγ̇u ‘thing’ + -ke (Ming 物件等, ‘and so forth’; the word ke is as in the glossary’s jaγ̇u-ke-ben, uncertain). in-ü is the genitive set after its noun (Ming 他的), ‘its’, meaning Zhongdu’s.

sentences.i: sent three men: Önggür the cook, Arqai-Qasar, and Shigi-Qutuqu.
sentences.n: baγ̇urči (Ming 厨子) ‘cook’ is set after Önggür’s name with Shiratori’s comma, as a title in apposition. γurban-i ‘the three’ takes the accusative. ilebe: ile- ‘send’ + -be (Ming 敎去了, with 敎, ‘caused to go’), as at §251.

sentences.t: Ede γurban-i aisai keġen Qada esergü uγdun

welcome, meeting (Ming 接 ‘receive’; stem uncertain) [接]

sentences.l: These three coming saying, Qada meeting, receiving
sentences.i: “These three are coming,” it was said; and Qada, to meet and welcome them,
sentences.n: aisai is ai- ‘come’ (stem uncertain) + -sai (Ming 來也 ‘is coming’). esergü (Ming 迎) is ‘facing, to meet’ and uγdun (Ming 接) ‘receive, welcome’; I know them only from the Ming. The quotation is not marked by Shiratori; the marks are mine, and who says it is not stated. The sentence runs on into the next unit.

bolt of cloth (the final n lost in print) [段匹]

sentences.l: Gold-having figure-having cloth-bolts having-taken, Zhongdu inside-from going-out, to-meet came.
sentences.i: took bolts of cloth worked with gold and with figures, came out from within Zhongdu, and came to meet them.
sentences.n: Possessive -tai: altatai is altan ‘gold’ + -tai, ‘gold-having’ (the n is lost), and hartai (Ming 紋有的 ‘pattern-having’; the Ming puts the first letter in brackets) I read as har ‘pattern’ + -tai. dotorāča is dotor ‘inside’ + ablative -āča. bariγ̇ad is bari- ‘seize’ + converb -γ̇ad. esergü irebe, ‘came to meet’, repeats the last words of the unit before.

sentences.t: Qada-da Šigi-Qutuqu ügülerün:

morph.gloss: Qada, a man’s name (Ming 人名) [人名 行]

sentences.l: Qada-to Shigi-Qutuqu speaking:
sentences.i: Shigi-Qutuqu said to Qada:
sentences.n: qada-da is Qada with the dative-locative -da (Ming 人名行 ‘to’). The speech that follows opens at the mark on Urida; Shiratori never closes it, and I close it in `i` where the sense ends, after the či that ends the rebuke.

sentences.t: "Urida ene Žuṅdu-jin ġed mün Žuṅdu Altan Qān-uγ̇ai ažuγ̇u-že.

morph.gloss: Zhongdu (Han 中都; Ming 北平), a capital [北平 的]
goods, property (printed ġed; read as ed from the Ming 物) [物]
Zhongdu (Han 中都; Ming 北平), a capital [北平]
Altan, ‘gold’; the Jin emperor’s title in Altan Qaγan (Ming 金) [金]
qan, ruler (short form beside qaγan) [皇帝的]
genitive-possessive: belonging to (Ming 的; ending uncertain)
sentence-final particle: it is so, indeed

sentences.l: "Formerly this Zhongdu’s goods, just Zhongdu, Altan Qan’s was-indeed.
sentences.i: “Formerly these goods of Zhongdu, and Zhongdu itself, belonged to the Altan Qan.
sentences.n: The Ming 物 on the third word shows that ġed is a misprint of ed ‘goods’; elsewhere in this part ġed in the glossary is a converb ending, which does not fit here. mün (Ming 只) is ‘just, the very’: ‘Zhongdu itself’. Qān-uγ̇ai is the title + -uγ̇ai (Ming 的), ‘belonging to’; ažuγ̇u-že is a- ‘be’ in the past + -že, ‘was indeed’. The -uγ̇ai ‘of’ ending is a pattern the next unit repeats.

sentences.t: Edöġe Žuṅdu Čiṅgis Qaγ̇an-uγ̇ai bi-že.

Chinggis, the title borne by Temüjin from 1206 [太祖︀]

sentences.l: Now Zhongdu Chinggis Qaγan’s is-indeed.
sentences.i: Now Zhongdu is Chinggis Qahan’s.
sentences.n: The contrast is built on the pair Urida … ažuγ̇u-že / Edöġe … bi-že: ‘formerly … was’, ‘now … is’. Qaγ̇an-uγ̇ai (Ming 皇帝 的) is the same possessive in -uγ̇ai. bi-že is bü- ‘be’ + -že.

sentences.t: Čiṅgis Qaγ̇an-u ed aγ̇urasu ečineġün jakin qulaγču abčiražü ögümü či.

morph.gloss: Chinggis, the title borne by Temüjin from 1206 [太祖︀]
genitive: of (after the n of a stem; back-vowel form)
bolt of cloth (the final n lost in print) [段匹]
secretly, behind (someone’s) back (Ming 背處) [背處]
to steal (stem inferred from the Ming 偷) [偷着]
to bring along (ab- ‘take’ + a second verb; form uncertain) [將着]

sentences.l: Chinggis Qaγan’s goods cloth-bolts secretly how stealing, bringing-along, giving you?
sentences.i: How can you steal the goods and cloth of Chinggis Qahan behind his back, bring them, and give them away?”
sentences.n: The rebuke. ečineġün (Ming 背處) ‘behind one’s back’; qulaγču is qulaγ- ‘steal’ (stem from the Ming 偷) + -ču; abčiražü ‘bringing’ (cf. §249); ögümü is ög- ‘give’ + a linking -ü- + -mü, which the Ming 與有 does not explain as a question; jakin ‘how’ makes it one. či ‘you’ is Qada. The speech has no closing mark in Shiratori; I close it here.

sentences.t: Bi ülü abqu keġežü Šigi-Qutuqu ese abuγ̇a.
sentences.l: I not take saying, Shigi-Qutuqu not-yet took.
sentences.i: Saying, “I will not take them,” Shigi-Qutuqu took none.
sentences.n: Two negatives to compare: bi ülü abqu, ‘I will not take’, is ülü + a participle in -qu (future), while ese abuγ̇a, ‘did not take’, is ese + a past verb (Ming 不曾要). That is the ese/ülü rule at work. abuγ̇a is abu- ‘take’ (Ming 要) + past -γ̇a. keġežü ‘saying’. The quotation marks are mine; Shiratori has none.

sentences.t: Öṅgür baγ̇urči, Arγai qojar abba.

morph.gloss: Arqai, a man’s name (short for Arγai-Qasar) [人名]

sentences.l: Önggür cook, Arqai the-two took.
sentences.i: Önggür the cook and Arqai, the two, took them.
sentences.n: Arqai is short for Arqai-Qasar (Ming 人名). baγ̇urči has Shiratori’s comma after it, as before. abba is ab- ‘take’ + -ba (Ming 要了). qojar ‘two’ follows the pair.

sentences.t: Ede γurban Žuṅdu-jin ed jaγ̇u-ke toγ̇olažu irebe.

sentences.i: The three counted up the goods and other things of Zhongdu, and came.
sentences.n: Ede (Ming 這(的每)) is ‘these’, the plural of ene; γurban here has no ending. toγ̇olažu is toγ̇ola- ‘count’ (Ming 數着) + -žu. irebe ‘came’; whom they come to is not stated.

sentences.t: Tende Čiṅgis Qaγan Öṅgür, Arγai, Qutuqu γurban-ača "Qada jaγ̇u ögbe" keġen asaγba.

sentences.l: There Chinggis Qaγan Önggür, Arqai, Qutuqu three-from "Qada what gave" saying asked.
sentences.i: Then Chinggis Qahan asked the three, Önggür, Arqai and Qutuqu, “What did Qada give?”
sentences.n: The ablative on the three, γurban-ača (Ming 行), is the person asked, ‘from the three’. The question is jaγ̇u ‘what’ (Ming 甚麽) with a plain past, ögbe; the marks are in Shiratori, and he adds no question mark. asaγba is asaγ- ‘ask’ + -ba (Ming 問了). tende ‘there, then’ (Ming 那裏). Qutuqu (Ming 人名) is the short form of Šigi-Qutuqu.

sentences.i: Shigi-Qutuqu said: “He brought bolts of cloth worked with gold and figures, and gave them.
sentences.n: The reply opens at Shiratori’s mark on Altatai and runs, with an inner quotation, to abulaγ̇a. ögülüġe is ög- ‘give’ + -ülüġe (Ming 與來), a past with a linking ü and the ending that is -luγ̇a after back vowels; the ‘he’ is Qada, the one asked about, and the text leaves him unnamed.

sentences.i: I said, ‘Formerly this Zhongdu belonged to the Altan Qan;

sentences.t: Edöġe Čiṅgis Qaγ̇an-uγ̇ai bolba-že.

sentences.i: now it has become Chinggis Qahan’s.’
sentences.n: bolba-že is bol- ‘become’ + -ba + -že, ‘has become indeed’ (Ming 做了 也者). Zhongdu, the subject, is dropped, as English can drop it.

sentences.i: You, Qada: how can you steal the goods of Chinggis Qahan behind his back and give them away?’ So saying, I took none.
sentences.n: The inner quotation ends with the rebuke repeated, and keġežü ‘saying’ closes it. bi ese abuba (abu- + -ba, Ming 要了, with ese ‘not yet’) is ‘I did not take’; ese + past once more, as against ülü + participle in the speech above. ögümü is the same form as in the first rebuke.

sentences.i: Önggür and Arqai, the two, took his gifts,” he said.
sentences.n: Hard. ögügsed-i is ög- ‘give’ + linking -ü- + the plural participle -gsed + accusative -i (Ming 與了的每行, ‘those given’), so ‘the things given’; in-ü is ‘his’ after its noun (Ming 他的), which I take to be Qada’s, though the Ming does not say whose; ‘his gifts’ is ‘his given things’. abulaγ̇a is abu- ‘take’ + -laγ̇a (Ming 了來). The closing mark is on abulaγ̇a, ending Shigi-Qutuqu’s reply; keġebe ‘said’ follows.

sentences.t: Čiṅgis Qaγan tende Öṅgür Arγai qojar-i maši doṅγodba.

sentences.i: Then Chinggis Qahan greatly blamed Önggür and Arqai, the two.
sentences.n: doṅγodba: the Ming 恠了 means ‘found strange, blamed’, so I read ‘blamed’. An earlier glossary entry has doṅγod- ‘make a sound’ for a different Ming (作聲). The stem is guessed. qojar-i is the pair with the accusative; maši ‘greatly’.

sentences.t: Šigi-Qutuqu-ji jeke josu sedkižüġü

past tense, final (Ming 了有; uncertain)

sentences.l: Shigi-Qutuqu-acc great principle thought-had.
sentences.i: He thought Shigi-Qutuqu a man of great principle.
sentences.n: josu (Ming 約速, glossed 理 ‘reason, right’) is ‘rule, principle’; jeke ‘great’. sedkižüġü is sedki- ‘think’ + -žüġü (Ming 了有, past; ending uncertain). The accusative on Šigi-Qutuqu-ji marks the man judged; whether the principle lies in him or in what he did, the sentence leaves open.

sentences.t: či keġen maši sojurγažu

morph.gloss: to show favour, bestow a grace [恩賜着]

sentences.l: you saying greatly showing-favour,
sentences.i: Calling him “you” and showing him great favour,
sentences.n: či keġen (Ming 你 麽道) is ‘saying “you”’, a form of address, and sojurγažu (sojurγa- ‘show favour’ + -žu, Ming 恩賜着) the converb. Shiratori has no opening mark for the speech; his closing mark falls after the second či in the next unit, and I put the opening at the start of the next unit’s English. The speech may instead begin at či here.

sentences.l: seeing’s my eye, hearing’s my ear, becoming, not-be? you"
sentences.i: “Will you not become my eye for seeing and my ear for hearing?”
sentences.n: Participles in -kü / -qu with the genitive -jin: üžekü-jin and sonosqu-jin are ‘of the seeing’, ‘of the hearing’, each followed by min-u (bi ‘I’ in its stem min- + -u) and the thing, nidün ‘eye’, čikin ‘ear’. bolžu ‘becoming’ and ülü-ü aqu: ülü ‘not’ + -ü (a question particle, uncertain; the Ming puts 麽 on the next word) and aqu (a- ‘be’ + -qu): ‘will you not be?’. The closing mark is Shiratori’s.

sentences.t: keġen žarliγ bolba.
sentences.l: saying decree made.
sentences.i: So saying, he issued a decree.
sentences.n: žarliγ bolba (Ming 聖旨 做了) is the house phrase ‘issued a decree’, here after the speech rather than before it; bolba is the finite verb, and keġen ‘saying’ ties the decree to the words just quoted.
